extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/epistemology and scientists reflecting on limits of knowledge
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length exposition arguing that human thought and scientific explanation are necessarily limited and relative, showing why consciousness, the self, the Infinite/Absolute, and ultimate scientific concepts cannot be comprehended. The text uses analytic arguments and illustrative scientific/biological examples to support its claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness is relational and continuous
rubrics_metrics.description: Any mental affection must be known in connexion with others — if it is not distinguished or identified by comparison with others, it is not recognized; a 'last state' of consciousness is impossible because recognition of relations presupposes later states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument shows that each state of consciousness is intelligible only through its relations to preceding states; the claim is illustrated by the impossibility of conceiving a final unrelatable mental state and compared to paradoxes about beginnings/ends of motion and rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inability to know duration of consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: We are unable either to believe or to conceive that the duration of consciousness is infinite, and equally unable either to know it as finite or to conceive it as finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from the relational/continuous nature of consciousness: both finite and infinite attributions run into logical or conceptual contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self/personality cannot be justified by reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief in the reality of personal existence is universal and unavoidable, yet it admits of no justification by reason; a true cognition of self is negated by laws of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Various hypotheses (self as subject underlying impressions; self as substance whose modifications are impressions; sceptical reduction to impressions alone) each imply contradictions or unresolvable assumptions. The argument invokes Mansel and Hamilton to show cognition of self would identify subject and object, annihilating both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate scientific ideas are symbols of incomprehensible realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Ultimate Scientific Ideas represent realities that cannot be comprehended; advancing explanation of explicate phenomena only brings out the inexplicableness of what remains behind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when phenomena are reduced to Force in Space and Time or to sensations, Force/Space/Time and sensations themselves remain inscrutable; the scientist encounters an insoluble enigma when pushing explanations to their ultimate terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought can only conceive the conditioned/relative
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind can conceive and therefore know only the limited and the conditionally limited; the unconditionally unlimited (the Infinite) and the unconditionally limited (the Absolute) cannot be positively construed to the mind — 'to think is to condition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from Sir William Hamilton: conceiving the Infinite or Absolute would require an infinite synthesis or an abandonment of the conditions of thought; thus highest generalizations remain finite and relative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness implies distinction and limitation; the Infinite is inconceivable
rubrics_metrics.description: The conception of consciousness necessarily implies distinction between one object and another, and distinction is limitation; hence the Infinite, which cannot be distinguished without limitation, is inconceivable and any consciousness of it is self-contradictory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawn from Hansel's exposition: attempting to ascribe positive attributes to the Infinite leads to mutual contradictions; the Infinite is better understood as the negation of the conditions of thought rather than a positive object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consciousness is essentially relational and cannot apprehend the Absolute
rubrics_metrics.description: Consciousness is possible only in the form of a relation (subject aware of object); to be conscious of the Absolute as such would require comparing what is conscious with that which is not — a contradiction — so we cannot be conscious of, nor know, the Absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because knowledge-as-consciousness always presupposes relation, any attempt to treat the Absolute (relation-free) as an object of thought collapses into self-contradiction; the Absolute may exist but cannot be conceived as such by us.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognition requires likeness, classification, and assimilation
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete act of consciousness implies not only distinction and relation but also likeness: a mental state must be known as of the same kind with previous states; classification (binding the like) is essential for orderly intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without assimilation of impressions into classes, successive mental states would be chaotic; recognition/assimilation underpins the possibility of ideas and knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding arises by assimilating particulars to known classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory understanding consists in disclosing a class of previously known cases with which a particular case can be assimilated (e.g., partridge rustle explained by known relation between disturbance and movement; respiration, levers, animal heat explained by general physical/chemical principles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several illustrative examples (partridge and wound/nerve; respiration and thoracic mechanics; levers; chemical origin of animal heat) show how explanation is achieved by inclusion in broader generalizations; this process repeatedly elevates particulars to general principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate explanations must terminate in the inexplicable
rubrics_metrics.description: If successive deeper interpretations are merely successive inclusions of special truths into more general truths, the most general truth — which admits inclusion in no other — cannot be understood; explanation must eventually bring us down to the inexplicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning about whether the explanatory process is limited or unlimited shows that a last, largest class cannot be interpreted; infinite synthesis would require infinite time, and a final generalization cannot be further explained, so comprehension reaches an unavoidable limit.
